top.title: Tokens per second to discoveries per hour: measured speed-versus-smarts curve for an evolutionary AI scientist, plus a replay simulator projected to faster chips (new idea 5; absorbs existing (e) and new idea 6)
top.description: An OpenEvolve-style loop (the LLM proposes a program, a sandbox scores it, the best programs feed the next prompt) runs on circle packing (n=26) with local vLLM models of three sizes, two precisions and three concurrency levels. Throttled runs of the same model change speed without changing quality, which separates the two. The team measures wall-clock and joules to a score threshold, then fits a replay simulator from per-call logs and checks it on a held-out configuration before projecting to a ~1,200 tok/s regime. This supersedes (e), which only breaks one loop down. Idea 6's prefix-cache layout can be added as one extra serving knob.
top.scores: compute-hardware 4, AI-scientist loop and generality 5, technical-judge appeal 5, visual 4, sponsor relevance 5, weekend feasibility 4, scientific honesty 4 (31/35)
top.verified: Opened: ThetaEvolve arXiv 2511.23473 reports 2.6359857 best with DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B, against AlphaEvolve 2.63586276. Its Table 6 compares 5.4 h with 63.6 h on 4 A6000s, but that run used ProRL-1.5B-v2, not the 8B model, so the ideator's attribution was wrong. Fractile's HPCwire release says ~40 tok/s on today's chips and that ~1,200 tok/s would 'compress that month into a day', with memory bandwidth as the bottleneck; it does not mention in-memory compute, precision or analogue. BaSE (arXiv 2605.29268) counts only effective FLOPs and LLM calls, not wall-clock. OpenEvolve accepts any OpenAI-compatible API via api_base and ships examples/circle_packing; per-call token and time logging is not documented, so the team adds it. Unverified: Kinetics paper claims, the OpenEvolve PR 2.634292 figure, the 1e-6 tolerance difference, and which hosted fast-inference APIs the event credits cover.
top.main_risk: Variance between runs is high, and small models may not reach 2.63 within a run budget. Lower thresholds (e.g. 2.60 and 2.62) and medians over 3 seeds are needed. If the evaluator dominates wall-clock, faster tokens barely help. That is still a valid Amdahl result, but it weakens the Fractile story, so cap evaluator time and report its share. The ~1,200 tok/s point is a model projection, not Fractile's chip.
top.headline_metric: Discovery speed-up per token-rate speed-up: how much faster an 8x tok/s range (same model, throttled) reaches sum of radii >= threshold, plus small-fast against large-slow time and joules to threshold, plus the replay simulator's error on a held-out configuration, then a labelled projection of 40 to 1,200 tok/s onto discovery time.

top.title: How many bits does an Ising machine need? An AI scientist stress-tests simulated-bifurcation hardware on GPU (new idea 2)
top.description: Thousands of batched simulated-bifurcation replicas run on Max-Cut (K2000, G-set) with fake-quantised couplings, low-precision state and injected analog noise. An agent maps a bits-against-noise phase diagram and tests hypotheses such as 'noise substitutes for lost precision below N bits'. Alongside, the team measures GPU spin-updates per second and time-to-target at fp32, bf16, fp16 and int8.
top.scores: compute-hardware 4, AI-scientist loop 4, technical-judge appeal 4, visual 5, sponsor relevance 3, weekend feasibility 5, scientific honesty 4 (29/35)
top.verified: Opened: Goto et al. 2021, Science Advances eabe7953. K2000 best cut estimated at 33,337, bSB on FPGA 0.26 ms and the CIM 1.1 s all confirmed. The ~2 ms dSB figure is time to the best value in Fig. 2B; dSB time-to-solution on K2000 is 1.3 s. The simulated-bifurcation PyPI package (2.0.0) supports device='cuda', agents, ballistic and discrete modes, and heated; it has no Max-Cut example. Close prior art: the ferroelectric CIM SB paper (arXiv 2512.17165) already sweeps state quantisation on K2000, from normalised cut 0.995 at interval 1/64 to 0.954 at interval 1. It does not give coupling bits or quantify noise. A search found no GPU study of coupling bit width against Max-Cut quality. arXiv 2610.06622 (abstract only) uses integer coupling sums but does not study precision. The SHNO paper's abstract (2110.08885) does not contain the claimed bit-resolution result, so that claim is unverified. The K2000 instance file was not located.
top.main_risk: It can read as 'just quantisation', and the state-precision sweep is already published, so the agent must find a non-obvious interaction (noise helps only below N coupling bits) and test it on both dense and sparse instances. The Fractile link is weak. If the exact K2000 instance cannot be found, use G-set best-known values instead.
top.headline_metric: Minimum coupling bit width that keeps >= 99% of the best-known cut at a fixed replica budget, against fp32, plus measured GPU time-to-target per precision, reported both batched and single-instance against the 0.26 ms FPGA figure.

top.title: (c) Existing: agent tunes a lattice Boltzmann blood-flow kernel with a physics gate and a live roofline plot
top.description: An agent rewrites and tunes an LBM GPU kernel. A physics check gates each version, and a live roofline plot shows achieved bandwidth. Fluid flow is easy for a technical judge to follow without biology.
top.scores: compute-hardware 5, AI-scientist loop 3, technical-judge appeal 4, visual 4, sponsor relevance 3, weekend feasibility 4, scientific honesty 4 (27/35)
top.verified: Not re-verified in this pass; it is an existing idea scored as a competitor.
top.main_risk: The agent is a kernel optimiser rather than a general hypothesis engine, and LLM kernel tuning is a crowded topic. It is aimed at GPU-vendor roofline thinking rather than at Fractile, ARIA or Inherent Labs.
top.headline_metric: Achieved fraction of peak memory bandwidth (MLUPS) of the agent's kernel against a reference LBM implementation, with the physics check passing.

top.title: How much analog noise can an LLM take? An AI scientist finds training-free fixes for in-memory LLM inference (new idea 1; same bits-and-noise question as existing (a), moved onto an LLM workload)
top.description: Batched noisy-inference simulations of Llama-3.2-1B under a PCM-like noise model with DAC and ADC quantisation. An agent ranks the non-idealities and tries mitigations: keeping sensitive projections digital, per-layer ADC bits, input centring and rotations, and recalibration. The output is a Pareto front of accuracy against a modelled hardware cost.
top.scores: compute-hardware 4, AI-scientist loop 4, technical-judge appeal 4, visual 3, sponsor relevance 5, weekend feasibility 3, scientific honesty 3 (26/35)
top.verified: Opened: Analog Foundation Models (arXiv 2505.09663). Llama-3.2-1B drops from 45.49 to 35.68 and Phi-3-mini from 70.03 to 62.02 under PCM noise with 8-bit DAC and ADC; retrained models reach 40.91 and 66.22; retraining took 96 V100s for ~90 h and ~230 h. All confirmed. The paper's code repository has only a generation example and an undocumented apply_noise_model.py; no evaluation pipeline is documented. AIHWKit-Lightning is described as a hardware-aware training toolkit with CUDA and Triton kernels for V100, A100 and H100; for inference simulation it exports to AIHWKit. Killer prior art found: Karfakis and Gupta (arXiv 2611.08693) recover accuracy without retraining using input centring plus Hadamard rotations, taking Phi-4 from 27.0 to 72.2 on ReRAM with 6-bit ADCs, within 2.2 points of floating point. NORA (DATE 2025, abstract only) keeps OPT-6.7b within 1% loss by rescaling, against ~30% without; whether NORA needs training is not stated.
top.main_risk: 'Training-free fixes' are already published, including the rotation method from this month, so the result can only be 'the agent rediscovers or matches Karfakis-Gupta and NORA autonomously'. Fractile's precision and whether it is analogue are not public. The inference noise tooling may require hand-writing the noise injection. Benchmark evaluation over many seeds is slow.
top.headline_metric: Share of the 45.49 to 35.68 Llama-3.2-1B drop the agent recovers without retraining at <= X% of weights kept digital, against HILAL-style sensitivity allocation and against the published centring-plus-Hadamard method.

top.title: Speculative experiments: a small model guesses the AI scientist's next shift-and-stack search on faint-asteroid detection while the large model thinks (new idea 7)
top.description: Speculative execution applied to the scientist loop. A small draft model proposes the next velocity search, the GPU runs it during the large model's reasoning, and the result is kept only if the large model picks the same experiment. The demo uses one of the event's own listed challenges (faint-asteroid detection).
top.scores: compute-hardware 3, AI-scientist loop 4, technical-judge appeal 4, visual 5, sponsor relevance 4, weekend feasibility 2, scientific honesty 4 (26/35)
top.verified: Opened: the KBMOD paper (arXiv 1901.02492) searches 10^10 trajectories in stacks of 10-15 4Kx4K images in under a minute on one consumer GPU and found 39 new KBOs. Speculative Actions (arXiv 2510.04371) reports up to 55% next-action accuracy and up to 20% latency reduction, lossless for the core framework. DualSpec's 3.28x was not opened (unverified). The KBMOD build requirements were not opened in this pass.
top.main_risk: Exact-match commits may rarely hit, and matching within a tolerance changes results. The gain exists only if one search takes about as long as the large model's thinking. KBMOD's CUDA build may fail on the event driver, so a PyTorch shift-and-stack fallback is needed. The hardware result is mostly about scheduling, not chips.
top.headline_metric: Wall-clock to 90% recovery of injected objects at a fixed false-positive count, speculative against sequential, with identical final detections, plus wasted speculative GPU-seconds and joules.

top.title: When does a thermodynamic computer beat a GPU? An AI scientist finds which analog imperfections move the crossover (new idea 4)
top.description: A batched GPU simulation of noisy coupled-oscillator (Langevin) hardware with component mismatch, ADC bits and noise. An agent finds which imperfection limits accuracy and how to calibrate it out. The crossover against a dense GPU solve measured on the event GPU is then recomputed.
top.scores: compute-hardware 3, AI-scientist loop 4, technical-judge appeal 3, visual 4, sponsor relevance 4, weekend feasibility 3, scientific honesty 3 (24/35)
top.verified: Opened: Melanson et al. (arXiv 2312.04836). The projected crossover at d ~ 3000 against an RTX A6000 (JAX Cholesky sampling) is confirmed, under a 1 us time constant, 10 MS/s ADCs, ideal 16-bit components and ~0.005 mW per cell, with ~10x at d = 10,000; it is a projection, not a measurement. Also confirmed: an 8-cell inversion error floor attributed to capacitance tolerance, sample variance rising monotonically and corrected by per-cell rescaling, and Table 1 of fitted L, R, kappa0 and C per cell. thermox was not opened.
top.main_risk: Validation is mostly qualitative because the 8-cell errors are only plotted. Energy rests on assumed ADC power. The judges may not know thermodynamic computing. Most of the hardware number is simulated; only the GPU baseline is measured.
top.headline_metric: Crossover dimension at equal accuracy with realistic imperfections, against the published ideal-device d ~ 3000.

verdict.recommended: Build new idea 5: tokens per second to discoveries per hour. It tests Fractile's own public claim, that ~40 to ~1,200 tok/s turns a month into a day, on a real AI-scientist loop running on the event GPU. That gives a measured result an inference-chip or serving engineer cares about: how much faster tokens actually speed up discovery, and where Amdahl's law stops it. The same result fits Inherent Labs (resource use of an AI scientist) and ARIA's simulator pillar (the replay simulator predicts performance of algorithm-plus-hardware pairs). The loop is task-agnostic, with circle packing as its demonstration, and the circle-packing demo is visual and needs no biology. Published scores to validate against: AlphaEvolve 2.63586276 and ThetaEvolve 2.6359857. It also beats the tabled idea (e), because it changes the hardware knob and measures the causal effect instead of only breaking one loop down. Keep throttling of the same model as the main experiment, so the result is not confounded by model quality. Backup if the GPU or vLLM setup fails by hour 4: new idea 2 (Ising bits), which is the safest build. Biology spin is optional: one slide by the medical student on why time-to-discovery, not tok/s, is the number that matters for an AI scientist doing drug or clinical research.
verdict.plan_26h:
Roles: E1 (agent-systems engineer) owns the loop: OpenEvolve on circle packing, vLLM endpoints, per-call logging (input and output tokens, latency, evaluator seconds, accepted or not), seeds and run orchestration. E2 owns measurement and the simulator: NVML power sampling, achieved bandwidth (weight and KV bytes per token divided by time, against the GPU peak), a token-rate throttle proxy (adds delay to the token stream), the replay simulator, and the live dashboard (circles plus racing best-score-against-time curves plus a roofline dot per configuration). M (medical student) owns the pitch, the one-sentence claim, the judge Q&A sheet, run bookkeeping and plots-to-slides, and the optional one-slide medical framing.

H0-2: find out the GPU type and count. Serve Qwen-class 0.5B, 1.5B and 7-8B through vLLM. Get the OpenEvolve circle-packing example running against the local endpoint. GO/NO-GO at H2: one full loop iteration logged end to end. If NO-GO, switch to Ising idea 2 (simulated-bifurcation on CUDA plus a fake-quant kernel).

H2-5: pilots of 45 minutes each per model. Fix thresholds at the best scores the 7-8B model reaches in 30-45 minutes (expected around 2.60-2.62; do not assume 2.63). Measure the evaluator's share of wall-clock and cap evaluator time. GO/NO-GO at H5: some model crosses the threshold in under 45 minutes. If not, lower the threshold, or use a smaller n or a faster evaluator.

H5-16: main grid, run in parallel across GPUs. (a) Speed-only axis: the same model throttled to 1x, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8 of measured tok/s. (b) Speed-against-quality axis: 3 model sizes x {FP16, 4-bit}. (c) Concurrency 1, 16, 64 (optional: prefix-cache layout as one extra knob). 3 seeds per cell, 45-minute cap; record time and joules to threshold. E2 builds the replay simulator from the logs in parallel.

H16-19: fit the simulator on the throttled runs, then predict one held-out real configuration (e.g. 4-bit 7B). GO at H19 if the error is <= 20%; otherwise report the error honestly and drop the 1,200 tok/s projection to a sensitivity band.

H19-22: project 40 to 1,200 tok/s onto time-to-discovery, labelled as a model. Final plots; dashboard replaying real logs (no live dependency).

H22-26: freeze code; rehearse a 3-minute pitch; build a backup video of the demo; write the Q&A answers: 'GPU is not Fractile's chip' (we measure loop sensitivity, not chip speed); 'batch changes latency and throughput' (we report which one the loop is sensitive to); 'model size confounds quality and speed' (the throttle axis isolates speed).

Headline numbers to report:
(1) Discovery elasticity: time-to-threshold against tok/s over the 8x throttle range (e.g. 8x tokens gives Nx faster discovery).
(2) Small-fast against large-slow wall-clock and joules to the threshold.
(3) Measured achieved bandwidth as a fraction of the GPU peak per configuration.
(4) Replay-simulator error on the held-out configuration.
(5) Projected discovery time at 1,200 tok/s against 40 tok/s, with the evaluator's share as the Amdahl ceiling.
(6) Best sum of radii reached, against AlphaEvolve 2.63586276 and ThetaEvolve 2.6359857 (constraint tolerance fixed).
killed: New idea 3 (LLMCompass memory-first chip design): the least visual idea, and agent-driven design-space search is crowded (AgentDSE and LLM-DSE from snippets only). The GPU only takes measurements; LLMCompass itself runs on CPU.

New idea 6 (cache-shared hypothesis swarm): prefix caching is a stock vLLM feature, and decode-heavy outputs may save little. Folded into idea 5 as one optional serving knob. The R3 abstract (arXiv 2604.11109) did not confirm the prompt-reordering claim the ideator attributed to it.

New idea 8 (co-scheduling LLM and Gray-Scott on one GPU; finalist score 23/35): NVIDIA's MPS docs cap thread share and pinned memory but say nothing about memory-bandwidth partitioning, and MPS daemon access in event containers is doubtful. Packing many runs into one job overlaps (b), and the classifier rather than the agent does the science. The 19-class Munafo catalogue was verified.

Existing (a) (heart-tissue bits and noise): biology-heavy for judges who do not know biology. Its bits-and-noise question is asked more relevantly by idea 1 (LLM inference, Fractile) and idea 2 (Ising hardware, ARIA).
Existing (b) (4,095 ECG lead subsets in one GPU job): batch packing with no real hypothesis loop, and the biology framing does not land with technical judges.
Existing (d) (routing between surrogate, coarse and full simulation): fits Callosum, but multi-fidelity routing is generic and gives no measured chip result. Below the top 6.
Existing (e) (time and energy breakdown of an AI-scientist loop): superseded by idea 5, which varies the hardware knob and validates a predictive simulator instead of only breaking one loop down.
